kas0: Groin Strain: First Steps, Exercises and Returning to Sport | İhsan Eren
kas1: What causes pain in the groin and inner thigh, what should you do in the first few days, and when can you run and return to sport? Warning signs and four exercises to strengthen the inner thigh.
kas3: Did pain start in your groin or inner thigh after a sudden change of direction, a twist or a kick in football, or a slip on a wet floor? This is usually a groin strain caused by overstretching the inner thigh muscles. With the right care in the first few days and then gradual strengthening exercises, most people improve noticeably within a few weeks.

kas16: Early, gentle movement: Move your leg gently as far as is comfortable; this prevents stiffness and loss of strength.

kas19: Four exercises to strengthen the inner thigh
kas20: Start after the first 48–72 hours. Do them little and often; some mild discomfort is fine, but the exercises should not make your pain noticeably worse. Increase the repetitions as they get easier.
kas22: Lie on your back with your knees bent and your feet in line with your knees. Place a ball or pillow between your knees and gently squeeze by pressing your knees together.
kas23: Hold for 5 seconds, 10–20 repetitions, twice a day
kas25: In the same position, with the ball or pillow between your knees, squeeze your buttock and tummy muscles to lift your hips. Gently squeeze the ball as you rise, hold for a few seconds, then lower slowly.
kas28: Lie on your painful side. Bend your top leg and rest that foot on the floor in front; keep your bottom leg straight. Keeping your hips still, lift the bottom leg, hold for 5 seconds and lower.
kas30: Pulling the leg inwards with a resistance band
kas31: Tie a resistance band to a fixed point and loop it around the ankle of your painful leg. With your leg out to the side, pull it inwards until your knees touch, then slowly let it back out.
kas33: What should I do if exercising hurts?
kas34: Some mild discomfort is acceptable, but the exercises should not make your symptoms noticeably worse. If an exercise is too painful, reduce the repetitions or how often you do it; if it still hurts, stop and ask a doctor or physiotherapist for advice.
kas36: Use ice for the first 2–3 days: apply ice or a bag of frozen peas wrapped in a damp towel for 15–20 minutes every 2–3 hours, taking care to avoid ice burns. During this time avoid hot baths, heat packs, alcohol and massage, as they can increase swelling.
kas37: When can I run and return to sport?
kas38: Most strains improve noticeably within about 2 weeks. To avoid further damage, it is advised to avoid strenuous exercise such as running for up to 8 weeks; severe strains can take months to heal. It is safest to return to sport gradually, with a physiotherapist, once you can walk without pain and your strength has almost fully returned.
kas40: If needed, you can use crutches or another walking aid for a short time in the first few days. As it becomes comfortable, start moving your leg gently while protecting it; early, gentle movement supports healing and prevents stiffness and loss of strength.
